title: I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on
description: When we talk about raising successful kids, we tend to talk about what they can do.Are they getting good grades? Are they going to basketball practice
body: When we talk about raising successful kids, we tend to talk about what they can do.Are they getting good grades? Are they going to basketball practices and winning games? Did they clean their rooms and set the table? Are they motivated? Responsible? Social? Can they solve problems, make good choices and eventually become independent adults?But after years spent working with more than 200 families, I've seen that some of the most important lessons children need to live successful, happy and fulfilling lives — and to build healthy relationships — have very little to do with action or achievement.Children absorb crucial messages in ordinary moments based on how we respond when they struggle, fail, disagree with us, disappoint us or simply become someone different from who we imagined they would be. In my experience, there are six things parents of the most successful, confident, resilient and well-adjusted kids teach them early on that have nothing to do with accomplishments.1. Failure doesn't change who they are to youChildren notice what happens between you when something goes wrong. They see your face when the grade comes back. They notice whether you seem prouder after the win and more distant after the loss.A child should be able to fail without feeling they have fallen in your eyes. For example, instead of immediately asking "Why didn't you study more?" try "I know you wanted a different result. How are you feeling about it?"When children know a bad result won't change how we see them, they don't have to be so afraid of getting things wrong. Failure can become something they learn from instead of something they feel they need to hide.2. Disappointing someone doesn't always mean they did something wrongIf being "good" means pleasing other people, someone else's disappointment can start to feel like proof a child did something wrong. They may learn to read the room before they learn to read themselves. We can show them a different way. You might say: "Someone else can be disappointed in your choice, and it can still be the right choice for you."Your child needs to know that you can disagree with them and they can still trust themselves. That matters later, too, with friends, partners and bosses.3. What they're good at isn't who they areEven positive labels can feel like pressure. If adults keep saying:"You're so smart." "You're our athlete." "You're the responsible one."A child can quietly start to hear: This is who I have to keep being. Then a B isn't just a B. Getting cut from the team isn't just disappointing. Struggling can start to feel like losing a piece of who they are.Instead of making the achievement their identity, notice what went into it. You might say: "You kept going even when that got difficult."When we separate what children accomplish from who they are, we give them room to become more than whatever they happen to be good at today.4. They can disagree or be upset with someone and still be lovedChildren need to disagree with us sometimes and discover that the relationship is still okay.That doesn't mean they make every decision. We are still the parents. We can hold a boundary with our kids and stay connected to them at the same time. You might say: "You're allowed to be angry with my decision. The answer is still no, and we're still okay."A child shouldn't have to choose between having a voice and feeling close to us. If they feel like they have to give up their voice to stay connected at home, saying no can become much harder everywhere else too.5. Uncomfortable feelings don't need to be fixed right awayOur instinct as parents is often to make our children feel better. We fix, reassure, distract or tell them everything will be fine. Sometimes they need something simpler: "This is hard. I'm here."Children need to learn that feeling bad doesn't mean something has gone wrong. They can be embarrassed and get through it. They can be nervous and still walk into the room. We don't have to rescue children from every uncomfortable feeling. Sometimes staying beside them as they experience those feelings is how they discover: I can handle this.6. Home is the one place they don't have to impress anyoneChildren already live in a world that measures them: grades, teams, rankings, likes and eventually college admissions, job offers and performance reviews.The outside world will keep asking: "What can you do?" Home should answer a different question with an emphatic yes: Do I still matter when there's nothing to celebrate?Sometimes it helps to say it directly: "I love watching you succeed. But you never have to impress me to belong here."Achievement should add to a child's life. It should never become the only reason they feel worthy.Reem Raouda is a certified conscious parenting coach, speaker and author dedicated to one core idea: that loving your child and making them feel safe are not the same thing. She is the founder of The Safe Mom and creator of The Safe Mom Masterclass, helping parents raise emotionally healthy children through emotional safety, connection and self-awareness. Find her on Instagram.

schema.headline: I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on

title: China's third-quarter economic growth quickens to 4.5% as exports surge, beating estimates
description: HONG KONG, CHINA - OCTOBER 17: People walk along the waterfront beneath Chinese national and Hong Kong regional flags, while others take photographs b
body: HONG KONG, CHINA - OCTOBER 17: People walk along the waterfront beneath Chinese national and Hong Kong regional flags, while others take photographs beside the harbour, with the city's skyline behind them, on October 17, 2026 in Hong Kong, China.  Cheng Xin | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesChina's economic growth accelerated to 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, as foreign demand for the country's technological goods largely offset a deepening property slump and sluggish consumer demand.  That compares with a 4.4% expansion forecast among economists polled by Reuters and the three-year low of 4.3% in the second quarter. The data shows an economy still leaning on factories and overseas buyers while households and private investors hold back. Growth through the first nine months averaged 4.6%, near the lower end of Beijing's official target range of 4.5% to 5%.For the first nine months this year, fixed asset investment in urban areas deepened declines, falling 7.2% from the same period a year earlier, compared with a 7.3% drop in Reuters poll.   In September, retail sales eked out a 1.1% growth, exceeding analysts' forecast for 0.6% increase, while industrial output grew 5.5% from a year earlier, in line with the forecast of 5.5% growth. The urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2% in September. Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as investment in AI-related sectors cools and trade tensions with the European Union escalate.Chinese authorities have stepped up policy support, including a package of targeted rate cuts and mortgage subsidies in late September. In early October, it also allocated 550 billion yuan of unused debt quota to local governments. Economists largely expect the People's Bank of China to hold benchmark lending rates unchanged through this year, leaving fiscal measures to do most of the work. Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that quarterly GDP growth was 4.5%.

schema.headline: China's third-quarter economic growth quickens to 4.5% as exports surge, beating estimates

title: India’s Finance Minister blames easy exits and excess liquidity for equity market's underperformance
description: Nirmala Sitharaman, India's finance minister, during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thu
body: Nirmala Sitharaman, India's finance minister, during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesExcess liquidity in India's equity market has contributed to underperformance and may continue to do so, according to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman."Because of the ease of liquidity, ease of availability, people are even exiting easily" from equities, Sitharaman told CNBC in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday. However, the fundamentals of the Indian economy are "fine," she said.Since January, India's key benchmark indexes have slipped nearly 12%, as per LSEG data, even though the country's economic growth has been resilient amid trade uncertainty and geopolitical shocks. India has been hit with record outflows by foreign investors from its equity markets, and Sitharaman said that continued capital outflows are one of the biggest risks for India in 2027. Still, domestic capital continues to flood the market. Indian equity mutual funds have recorded net inflows every month since March 2021, according to data released by industry body Association of Mutual Funds in India earlier this month.Multinational companies, private equity funds and foreign investors have been able to make partial or full exits from their investments at a premium. Between 2021 and 2025, Indian initial public offerings collectively raised $60.4 billion, of which "a staggering" $37.7 billion, or 63% of total proceeds, went to existing holders who sold their shares to the public, an EY report in August said.Anti-AI PlayForeign portfolio investors have sold direct Indian equities of over $33 billion so far this year, as per Indian depository firm NSDL. India has gained a reputation as an anti-artificial intelligence trade, while markets like Taiwan and Korea, with AI champions, have attracted strong investment flows.The flight of capital toward AI and the U.S., which otherwise moves toward different countries for different sectoral investments, is "a concern," she added. Taiwan now has the largest market weighting in the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index at 29%, while Korea has moved into second place at 22%, as per a report by Goldman Sachs on Oct. 8. India's share has compressed from 19% a few years ago to 10%, it added.But with the global AI rally showing cracks, Sitharaman said India wouldn't be "hurt" from any spillover if the bubble burst. India has not received the "AI kind of investments coming into different jurisdictions," she said. Sitharaman, who is India's longest-serving finance minister to hold the office continuously, added that the South Asian country was "no longer a laggard" in the frontier tech space and investment was being made to set up semiconductor manufacturing.

schema.headline: India’s Finance Minister blames easy exits and excess liquidity for equity market's underperformance

title: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
description: An electronic display shows the national debt in Washington, Aug. 19, 2026.Mandel Ngan | AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with
body: An electronic display shows the national debt in Washington, Aug. 19, 2026.Mandel Ngan | AFP | Getty ImagesThe U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress. The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, the Treasury Department reported Friday.  It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official.With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001.Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week.Where the debt comes fromSocial Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025.Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025.Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives  – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion.Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year.In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owed exceeded $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade.  Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can "grow our way out of" its increasing debt pile."Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August.President Donald Trump pitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional.The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due to refunds required following the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers.The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

schema.headline: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year

title: China's CXMT sees shares drop over 6% as investors look past chipmaker's profit turnaround
description: QINGDAO, CHINA - SEPTEMBER 04: A general view shows facilities related to Changxin Memory Technologies on September 4, 2026 in Qingdao, Shandong Provi
body: QINGDAO, CHINA - SEPTEMBER 04: A general view shows facilities related to Changxin Memory Technologies on September 4, 2026 in Qingdao, Shandong Province of China. The company's global DRAM market share has exceeded 10 percent following increased production capacity at its Hefei and Beijing lines, positioning it as the fourth-largest supplier worldwide while advancing research and development in advanced processes and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). (Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images)Vcg | Visual China Group | Getty ImagesShares of ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, fell 6.5% Monday even as the company on Friday forecast a sharp swing to profitability for the first nine months of 2026.CXMT said in a filing Friday that it expects net profit attributable to shareholders of between 131 billion yuan ($19.58 billion) and 132.5 billion yuan for the January-to-September period, reversing a net loss of 5.28 billion yuan a year earlier, according to a Google translation of the filing.The company expects revenue of around 265 billion yuan to 270 billion yuan, an increase of 232.9 billion yuan to 237.9 billion yuan from the same period a year earlier.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconShares of CXMT on 19 Oct. The company attributed the sharp improvement to rapidly growing demand for AI computing power since the second half of 2025, which has boosted the global DRAM market, leading to supply shortages and significant price increases, according to the filing. CXMT has been gaining ground in the global memory chip market, challenging established players including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology. The Chinese chipmaker accounted for 10% of global DRAM revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5% a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research's data last month.

schema.headline: China's CXMT sees shares drop over 6% as investors look past chipmaker's profit turnaround

title: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
description: A Citibank branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market
body: A Citibank branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said. The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said.China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments. Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said. Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters. One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100. The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon. Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November. "The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group. Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

schema.headline: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
description: KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has
body: KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."Beverage cups stacked inside a Yum Brands KFC restaurant in Shelbyville, Kentucky, Jan. 29, 2021.Luke Sharrett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFor many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas. Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

schema.headline: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades

title: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
description: South Korean Finance Minister nominee Lee Hyoung-il speaks during his confirmation hearing at the National Assembly in Seoul, South Korea, Sept. 15, 2
body: South Korean Finance Minister nominee Lee Hyoung-il speaks during his confirmation hearing at the National Assembly in Seoul, South Korea, Sept. 15, 2026.Kim Hong-ji | ReutersThe semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said on Saturday. "For now, our view is that we can sustain this growth at least through next year," Lee told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "That's because the gap between demand and supply for semiconductors is still very wide, and supply is still being expanded."His comments come after semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. South Korean chip stocks like SK Hynix and Seoul Semiconductor were part of the sell-off, along with U.S. giants like Nvidia.Chip stocks' large weighting has fueled volatility in South Korea's stock market this year, Lee said. He attributed the market's wild swings to the semiconductor industry's larger share of the economy than in other countries. Despite the market swings, South Korea's economy is "solid," Lee said.On Thursday, an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper, a prominent South Korean publication, urged the country's government to prepare for the coming slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. The author said two experts expect a "flood of new supply" of semiconductors that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" by 2029, according to a CNBC translation.Read more CNBC tech newsApple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the testTrump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in UkraineBlue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launchesSpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized imagesWhile South Korea's semiconductors may be driving volatility in its stock market, the industry has also fueled tax growth. Lee said the country expects to collect more taxes than initially projected this year. South Korea will ultimately be in a stronger fiscal position because of the chip boom, he added.WATCH: Don't overlook opportunity in South Korea, says Verdad Advisers' Rasmussenwatch now

schema.headline: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says

title: 'Everyone laughed' when he started a pumpkin farm—now it brings in $2 million a year
description: Three decades ago, when Kelly Schultz announced his intention to start a pumpkin farm, "everybody laughed at me," he says. Schultz, a second-generatio
body: Three decades ago, when Kelly Schultz announced his intention to start a pumpkin farm, "everybody laughed at me," he says. Schultz, a second-generation antique seller, had no prior experience with farming when he bought a small farm in Clarence, New York, in 1993.Nobody thinks he's out of his gourd now.Schultz, 74, is the owner and operator of The Great Pumpkin Farm, a seasonal attraction about 15 miles northeast of Buffalo that draws over 100,000 visitors each fall. The Great Pumpkin Farm brought in $2 million in annual revenue in 2025, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It — and it's open just seven weeks a year. This year, the farm is open to visitors between Sept. 19 and Oct. 31, and they're not just coming to buy pumpkins. With a $20 weekend admission ticket, fall enthusiasts can ride the farm's pumpkin-themed train, explore its giant corn maze and compete in pie-eating contests, among other attractions.Halloween is big business for Schultz and other seasonal business owners. Halloween-related spending is expected to reach $13.5 billion in the U.S. in 2026, according to a consumer survey by the National Retail Federation published in September. Among the 74% of Americans celebrating the holiday this year, 42% said they plan to carve a pumpkin.At The Great Pumpkin Farm, "attendance is increasing just about every year," according to Schultz.During the fall, "there are people that come here almost every weekend," he says. "They love it so much, they just keep coming back."A giant pumpkin put them 'on the map'Schultz, who runs an antique store and an antique auction business year-round, says he was inspired to start his farm after visiting a pumpkin patch in upstate New York in the early 1990s. That farm had "muddy parking lots and not a whole lot of restrooms," he recalls, but there were "a zillion people" walking around and buying pumpkins. "I looked around and I said, 'I could do this, better than this,'" Schultz says. So when the old cow farm next to his antique store went up for sale, he bought the 85-acre property for approximately $650,000, he says.With the help of other local farmers, Schultz learned how to grow his own gourds, and The Great Pumpkin Farm officially opened in 1996. But Schultz had even bigger plans for his farm. That same year, he asked Ray Waterman, founder of the World Pumpkin Confederation, an organization dedicated to growing giant pumpkins and squash, to host his annual World Pumpkin Weigh-Off at The Great Pumpkin Farm.Schultz bought prize indemnity insurance, which covers the cost of contest and promotion prizes, and offered $50,000 to anyone who brought in a pumpkin that weighed 1,000 pounds or more. He took out ads in papers "across the country" to promote the weigh-off. The winning pumpkin, grown by a couple from Lowville, New York, broke the world record at the time at a whopping 1,061 pounds.The Great Pumpkin Farm hosted its first pumpkin weigh-off in 1996. Courtesy of Kelly Schultz"We were in magazines and newspapers all over the world," Schultz recalls. "That put us on the map right off the bat." The Great Pumpkin Farm still hosts a weigh-off event every October, and this year's heaviest pumpkin weighed a whopping 1,908.5 pounds, almost double the weight of the 1996 winner.Hay rides, pumpkin cannons and moreThese days, Schultz focuses less on growing gourds — to keep up with demand, he purchases most of the farm's pumpkins from nearby farms. But The Great Pumpkin Farm's 50-foot pumpkin pyramid, which is visible from the road, is still the first thing that incoming visitors see. According to Schultz, the farm stocks over 25,000 pumpkins each year.Visitors pick out pumpkins to purchase at The Great Pumpkin Farm.William Muench | CNBC Make ItWeekend visitors pay $20 per ticket, which covers admission for both days. They can access a vast range of activities including hayrides, pie-eating contests, magic shows, a giant slide, live music, train rides, a kid-friendly "boo barn" and pumpkin pedal kart rides, just to name a few.For an extra fee, visitors can try the farm's amusement rides, pumpkin cannons, zombie paintball train, carnival games and Buffalo Bills-themed corn maze. Alongside the farm's bar and bakery, Schultz hosts festival food vendors whose offerings range from barbecue to specialty grilled cheese sandwiches."You can come out here and spend the day and still not have done everything," he says.Weekdays require no admission charge, and are more low-key. Visitors can purchase pumpkins, visit the Halloween store, bar and bakery, and enjoy the outdoor playground, petting zoo and hay maze. Schultz brings in petting zoo animals for the farm's fall festival.William Muench | CNBC Make ItCreating this fall festival requires a huge amount of labor, according to Schultz. He employs over 100 seasonal workers during the seven weeks the farm is open each year, and their job duties range from driving tractors for hay rides to serving pumpkin donuts.Rising gas costs are another major expense, Schultz says: It takes "lots and lots of gallons of fuel" to maintain the grounds and operate tractors for the hay rides. Since Schultz tries to avoid raising admission costs, he predicts that the business will "make a little bit less" in 2026. "The business has been profitable, but we generally take most of the money and try and put it back into it," Schultz says.For an extra admission fee, the farm also offers amusement rides and carnival games.William Muench | CNBC Make ItBecause Schultz owns the land surrounding the farm — approximately 300 acres in total — there's always room to expand, he says. Each year, he aims to add "something new, something fun, or upgrade what we already have."Creating a 'generational business'The farm has grown into a family operation: Schultz's son Ben has helped him run it, and his antique businesses, for the last 25 years."I just like hanging out with my dad, so that's how I got involved in all this," says Ben Schultz, 45. "I'm very proud of what he created here, and I'm just happy to be a part of it."Their shared goal for The Great Pumpkin Farm, according to Ben Schultz, is to "continue the momentum." From the farm's simple beginnings, "it's hard to imagine that it's gotten as big as it has," he says. Kelly Schultz's grandchildren have also started to help out around the farm, he says."They love coming here," he says. "They all want to be here all the time, every day." "I'm sure that the pumpkin farm will be a generational business," he continues. "It's definitely a family event."Kelly Schultz and his son Ben in front of The Great Pumpkin Farm's pumpkin pyramid.William Muench | CNBC Make ItThroughout October, the farm is buzzing with activity, but after Halloween, everything shuts down, according to Schultz. The petting zoo animals go back to their original farms; the amusement park rides are packed up and removed, and pig farmers pick up the remaining pumpkins to use for feed. Putting everything away and cleaning up the property takes approximately a month, Schultz says.For the rest of the year, around 20 full-time staff help maintain the Great Pumpkin Farm's old barn buildings and keep the grass mowed. Otherwise, it's back to selling antiques for Schultz and his family — at least until next fall.

schema.headline: 'Everyone laughed' when he started a pumpkin farm—now it brings in $2 million a year

title: Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks
description: A cyclist rides past the Meta sign outside the headquarters of Facebook parent company Meta Platforms in Mountain View, California, on Nov. 9, 2022.Pe
body: A cyclist rides past the Meta sign outside the headquarters of Facebook parent company Meta Platforms in Mountain View, California, on Nov. 9, 2022.Peter Dasilva | ReutersFears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.UnitedHealthHealth insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan. Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright. The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.Meta PlatformsSocial media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call. Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization."Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.Marvell TechnologyNext is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds. After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370. The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business. Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

title: The bloated workweek is coming for Sundays—as some embrace flexibility, others worry about job security
description: Alessia Montanaro is just about to close her second busy season of the year. Since September she's been logging up to 60 hours of work per week, somet
body: Alessia Montanaro is just about to close her second busy season of the year. Since September she's been logging up to 60 hours of work per week, sometimes going as late as 11 p.m., and making a habit of working Sundays from her home office.The 30-year-old works in public accounting in Austin, Texas, and has gotten used to these sprints around tax season. She's not the only weekend work warrior.For many office workers, Sundays have become the unofficial new start to their workweek: Nearly half of workers often clock in on Sundays, according to a recent report from Owl Labs, the video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July with a margin of error of 2%. Some 21% of people surveyed say they work the whole or nearly the whole day, and another 24% say they often do a few hours of work.  Of the remaining set of workers, 11% say they quickly check messages but don't really work, 18% say they rarely do any work on Sundays, and 26% say they never do.It's been six years since work for many moved home during the Covid-19 pandemic, opening the possibilities of logging hours anytime and anywhere there's Wi-Fi. While some people deprioritized work and put up strict boundaries to protect their personal time, tech use data shows that many years later, working time has bled into every hour of every day. Chat messages sent outside of the standard Monday through Friday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. workweek rose 15% year-over-year, now up to an average 58 messages per user, according to Microsoft's 2025 research on what it calls the rise of the "infinite workday." Among those working on the weekends, nearly 20% check their email before noon on a Saturday and Sunday, and over 5% are in their inboxes on Sunday nights, per Microsoft.As far as these online habits show, the sanctity of Sundays off may be vanishing as an always-on work culture takes over.Daytime distractions push work to the weekendSome Sunday workers say working weekends or after hours is the only way to get focused work done. During the workweek, "I get pulled in five different directions" with messages or requests from associates and higher-ups, Montanaro of Austin says.Working a distraction-free Sunday can help workers get more done, says Frank Weishaupt, CEO of Owl Labs. But it can also be a signal that the typical Monday-through-Friday is overloaded with busywork.The work of getting work done can be disruptive: Employees are interrupted roughly every two minutes during core work hours with meetings, emails or chat messages, according to Microsoft data. Some 38% of workers say they have meeting fatigue, with the most common gripes being that meetings are too long and there are too many of them, according to Owl Labs.Workers carve out flexibility where they canWeishaupt says Sunday work periods could be seen as a good thing "as it relates to the employee's desire for flexibility" and a growing interest in "microshifting," a term Owl Labs coined to mean working outside of a traditional Monday through Friday 9-to-5 time block.Microshifting can be especially helpful to moms, caregivers and anyone who might need to duck out for a few hours on workdays. Kylie Gonzalez, 29, says she'll clock into her account manager job from home on a Sunday if she took some time during the week for doctor's appointments, school pickup for her kids or other events.But she's wary of spending more than an hour or so working on the weekend, or making a habit of it. "Some companies may take advantage of that fact and add more to your plate because they see so much is being done," she says.Job anxiety fuels the Sunday scariesIn 2019, the norm was going into the office on a Monday and getting settled for the week ahead, Weishaupt says. That prep work is now shifting to Sundays."My Sunday evening feels awful because I'm just thinking about Monday and all the work that I didn't finish on Friday," says Tobi Collins, 28, a strategy consultant in Dallas. Her weekend work helps her curb the Sunday scaries, she says: "If I just get ahead of it, I'm not as nervous about the week."Dina Otero, 42, of Philadelphia, says she used to regularly log weekend hours, even spending her Sundays back from vacation catching up on emails before her actual return to work. Working a little extra at the start of the week would help her get ahead, she told herself. Really, it was just anxiety and "my own way of thinking that I had control over things that I really did not," she says.In the current tough job market, when companies are signaling layoffs before they happen, hiring less and raising expectations around artificial intelligence, Weishaupt says Sunday work could also be a sign of overworking when people are worried about job security. Workers are "doing anything they can to hug that job, and that may mean that they're just working a lot more, Sunday included," he says.That can become a big problem if unchecked. "If 40 hours become 60 hours, you know you're going to have burnout, you're going to have frustration, and then when that pendulum swings the other way, you're going to have a lot of churn," Weishaupt says.LaToya Allen, 45, in Washington, D.C., isn't sure the extra work hours are always worth it. She found herself in a burn-and-churn cycle in 2020, when she became disillusioned by her corporate tech job and what she saw as a false promise of success and security.She now runs her own boutique tech consultancy and says working "pretty much seven days a week" comes with the territory of entrepreneurship. For 9-to-5 workers, though, "I don't see how working on a Sunday is going to save your job," she says. "Just because your manager sees you working on Slack on a Sunday, what does that matter?"

title: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
description: A voter casts his ballot during early voting at the Polk County Election Office on Oct.14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa. Charlie Neibergall | Getty Images
body: A voter casts his ballot during early voting at the Polk County Election Office on Oct.14, 2026 in Des Moines, Iowa. Charlie Neibergall | Getty ImagesOne of the last big campaign-finance snapshots before the Nov. 3 Election Day is now available, and both political parties found something to like. But campaign cash is flowing in very different ways — and, on balance, points to an environment more favorable for Democrats.On one side, Democratic candidates have turned into absolute cash cows, raising oodles more than their Republican rivals across Senate and House battlegrounds.Republicans, however, still have a leg to stand on from an unprecedented flood of outside super PAC cash, bankrolled by a tiny circle of billionaires led by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The deluge of capital could be enough to stave off the worst of what has otherwise been a treacherous political environment for the GOP amid stubbornly high inflation and drooping approval ratings for President Donald Trump.A flurry of Federal Election Commission filings Thursday at a key deadline detailed what candidates raised and spent from July through September and give insight into many of the outside groups backing them. More of the outside-money picture comes next week with another deadline for additional filings. Here are CNBC's five takeaways:Democratic grassroots strength If Democrats want a financial case for a blue wave, start with the candidates themselves.Democratic Senate nominees put up gaudy third-quarter totals. James Talarico raised $60.2 million in Texas, Jon Ossoff brought in $33.1 million in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed raised $30.7 million in Michigan. Sherrod Brown brought in $23.1 million in Ohio, while Troy Jackson raised $20.4 million in Maine, Mary Peltola $14.1 million in Alaska and Roy Cooper $12.2 million in North Carolina.Even in reliably red Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised $9.4 million.In several of those races, the Republican numbers were not even close. Ken Paxton raised about $10.2 million in Texas, Mike Rogers $9.7 million in Michigan, Susan Collins $5.2 million in Maine and Jon Husted $4.8 million in Ohio.Candidate dollars are especially potent in the final stretch because campaigns control where they go and qualify for lower television advertising rates than super PACs do. In other words, Republicans may be able to make up a $1 fundraising gap with outside money — but it can cost them more than $1 to do it.The same fundraising edge stretches into the House.Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents through September in 13 of the 21 House races currently rated Toss Up by Cook, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. In North Carolina's 11th District, for example, Democrat Jamie Ager raised $2.1 million in the third quarter, compared with roughly $313,000 for Republican Jennifer Balkcom. The fundraising surge coincides with a shifting map: the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projected last week that Democrats could gain two to six Senate seats — enough to put the four-seat majority threshold within reach — and nine to 19 House seats, which would flip the chamber.Republicans' ace in the holeWhile Democratic candidates dominate direct donations, Republicans are countering with overwhelming outside spending.The Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC, raised a record $272.9 million from July through September, roughly $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart, according to FEC filings. On the House side, the Congressional Leadership Fund raised a record $94.4 million during the quarter and entered October with $156 million in cash, according to its FEC filing.That outside money is functioning as a financial backstop for GOP candidates who trail badly in direct fundraising. Texas is the most extreme example: the SLF funneled $158 million into Texas PAC, the super PAC backing Paxton, according to FEC filings. Elsewhere, Republicans have committed $15 million through the SLF to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Outside groups account for roughly 80% of all ad buys in Alaska, where the SLF has spent $14 million backing Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.The blitz allowed Republicans to hold an aired-ad advantage in seven of eight top Senate battles and 25 of 42 contested House seats rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report as of Oct. 9, according to AdImpact.But polls have shown little movement in recent weeks, despite the advantage.Elon Musk, chief executive officer of Tesla Inc., during the launch of America.gov in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMusk fights for TexasNo donor better captures the scale — or the leverage — of that outside-money advantage than the world's richest person, Musk.He pumped more than $276 million into federal political groups during the third quarter, making him the biggest known individual donor of the midterms. His disclosed giving included $158 million to Senate Leadership Fund and another $89 million to his America PAC, according to FEC filings. Most of that capital was earmarked for a single rescue mission: Texas, the state that's his primary residence and headquarters of his businesses.Musk gave the SLF $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23. Both times, the SLF transferred the exact same amount to Texas PAC the following day. The group, which is backing Paxton, reported no other donors through the end of September.Until now, many national Republicans had been reluctant to sink resources into the Lone Star state's expensive media market while fighting across an already expanded Senate map. Musk effectively erased that trade-off, supplying enough money to build a dedicated financial firewall around Paxton without forcing the party to pull resources from other battlegrounds.Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican candidate for the U.S. Senate, speaks to attendees during a campaign rally at Matt's Rancho Martinez on Tuesday, May 19, 2026, in Allen.Elías Valverde II | The Dallas Morning News | Getty ImagesDemocratic megadonors get off the sidelinesFor months, Democrats worried over the reluctance of traditional megadonors to write checks following the 2024 election cycle with presidential contest drama at the top of the ticket. The latest filings suggest that freeze is thawing — though much money is still bypassing the Democratic National Committee.Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna, put about $16 million into the midterm fight this summer, according to FEC filings, while LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who had also withheld money from the DNC this cycle, poured $11.5 million into the super PAC backing Talarico earlier this year.The renewed megadonor money gives Democrats another source of firepower for the final weeks that can be quickly redirected if needed. Already, Democrats' Senate Majority PAC raised a record $151 million in the third quarter and ended September with $112 million in cash, even as its Republican counterpart raised substantially more.Record-breaking moneyAll the spending is feeding an election on track to shatter spending records.AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising during the 2025-26 election cycle, which would make 2026 the most expensive cycle on record — surpassing both the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms and the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 presidential cycle.The congressional fight alone has already put $3.8 billion in advertising on the air, more than $870 million ahead of the comparable point in 2024, according to AdImpact. Senate races are helping drive the surge: the firm projects $3.4 billion in Senate advertising by the end of the cycle, up 48% from 2022.But as the amount of money rises, some of it is becoming harder for voters to trace back to its original source.Thursday's filings showed millions flowing into super PACs from nonprofits and other entities that are not required to disclose their own donors, leaving the original source of some of the cycle's biggest checks hidden.

schema.headline: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk

title: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely
description: LONDON, ENGLAND - JULY 7: Deputy Governor for Financial Stability, Sarah Breeden, attends the Bank of England financial stability report press confere
body: LONDON, ENGLAND - JULY 7: Deputy Governor for Financial Stability, Sarah Breeden, attends the Bank of England financial stability report press conference at Bank Of England on July 7, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Doug Peters - WPA Pool/Getty Images)Wpa Pool | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesHedge funds' increased presence in global bond markets makes the likelihood of a broader market shock "greater than what it was," Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC Thursday.Breeden — the central bank's deputy governor for financial stability, and a member of its rates-setting Monetary Policy Committee — said the changing mix of bond market investors, and their increased use of leverage, raises the risk of localized market turbulence turning into broader financial stress.watch now"One of the things that has become increasingly apparent over the last several years is that the investors in our core government bond markets globally have changed," Breeden told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah in an interview Thursday."It's not the real money investors, the insurance companies and pension funds, in the way it used to be. It's increasingly hedge funds, and those hedge funds are price-sensitive, leveraged, international. That, of course, means that the likelihood of a shock in one market transmitting to another is greater than what it was."Breeden was speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconU.S. 10-Year Treasurys.Hedge fund assets swellWith gross assets now standing at about $13 trillion, hedge funds have become an increasingly important part of the global investor landscape, the IMF said on Tuesday.  In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, published Tuesday, the IMF acknowledged hedge funds' role in supporting market liquidity and efficiency.But it also warned that the hedge fund industry's use of leverage to boost returns, and its tendency to pursue crowded trades, could turbo-charge market stress in times of turmoil. That, in turn, could spill over into broader financial markets, and areas such as banks' prime brokerage businesses, according to the IMF. "The source of the shocks are bond markets, and the likelihood of a spillover is higher than it was," Breeden said.Hedge funds' presence in the global government bond market — particularly their use of so-called "basis trades" — has come under sharper scrutiny this year, following the sharp sell-off in sovereign debt. Hedge funds held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025, according to U.S. Office of Financial Research data published on Aug. 19. Basis trades are an arbitrage bet in which hedge funds are positioned long in cash Treasurys while shorting their corresponding futures contracts, with the aim of profiting from the price gap. While the price differential between the two is relatively small, hedge funds often employ large amounts of leverage to further inflate returns.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconFrance 10-Year OATs.Earlier this month, 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels since 2002. Across the Atlantic, yields on 10-year U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also touched multi-decade highs.Yields on France's government bonds, known as OATs, have moved sharply higher in recent weeks amid rising concerns about the country's fiscal outlook — fueling fears of a fresh sovereign debt crisis impacting the euro zone.

schema.headline: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely

title: France hit by worst unrest in years as attempts to rein in government spending meet citizen ire
description: A protestor with a gas mask holds a French flag in front of a fire at the Boulevard des Capucines during a demonstration to protest against the "high
body: A protestor with a gas mask holds a French flag in front of a fire at the Boulevard des Capucines during a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", in Paris on October 17, 2026 as part of a nationwide call for mobilisation bringing together various groups expressing their anger.Kiran Ridley | Afp | Getty ImagesFrance endured its worst unrest in years this weekend as nationwide protests over high living costs and declining public services turned violent ahead of a key government vote on the budget.Demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, with almost 2,400 people arrested, shops looted or damaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country, according to the interior ministry. Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, the ministry said.President Emmanuel Macron, whose final months in office are increasingly defined by mounting political, fiscal and social discontent, ordered a review of whether there had been failings in intelligence gathering or police preparedness, and asked the government to bring together students, teachers, lawmakers, unions and business leaders this week to produce "concrete proposals" to address the crisis. The unrest comes as Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's minority government seeks €54 billion ($61 billion) of fiscal savings in its 2027 budget as he tries to narrow the country's growing deficit. The National Assembly is due to hold a formal vote on the first part of the bill on Tuesday. France has in recent years struggled to rein in spending and a debt burden that has ballooned to a record €3.6 trillion in the second quarter, reaching 119% of GDP, and is becoming increasingly expensive to service as interest rates spike across the world. About 550,000 people marched in scores of cities Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris, according to authorities. The latest wave of demonstrations followed a month-long student movement over teacher shortages and school conditions, with broader anger from unions. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted shops and attacked police. In a televised address Sunday evening, Macron said: "Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?""Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it," he said, pledging an "uncompromising" response to "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups, joined by numerous delinquents." He stopped short of declaring a state of emergency or imposing a curfew, but said prefects and mayors would be allowed to ban certain gatherings where necessary to protect public buildings and local businesses. The 143-year-old town hall in Limoges, in central France, was set ablaze and largely destroyed after looters broke the window in an arson attack. "There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives," shaken Mayor Guillaume Guérin told Reuters on Sunday. Protesters forced their way into Marseille's city hall, and a tourist office in Lyon was set ablaze. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Sunday that several hundred shops sustained considerable material damage, and Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores there were looted.One protester died of cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris, police said in a statement, without providing further details. Police fired tear gas and stun grenades Sunday afternoon to break up the rally at Place de la République in Paris, and bicycles were set on fire.  The country's economy minister Roland Lescure has vowed government support for business owners who have suffered losses from the riots. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos," Reuters reported, citing a statement. Far-right opposition leader Marine Le Pen, frontrunner for next year's presidential campaign, said the troubles showed that Macron's government is "running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented." Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is also running for president, said Macron needed to answer the demands of protesting high-school students, and the country could be heading toward "events that will eventually become uncontrollable."

title: Trump's Russia diesel deal may offer Putin more than money — and spell trouble for Ukraine
description: Ukraine is facing increasing uncertainty over its ability to sustain the war against Russia as a series of moves by U.S. President Donald Trump has ra
body: Ukraine is facing increasing uncertainty over its ability to sustain the war against Russia as a series of moves by U.S. President Donald Trump has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.Trump's agreement with Putin to ease sanctions for Russia to provide global markets with diesel, as well as restrictions on U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukrainian forces, has put President Volodymyr Zelenskyy  in a difficult position as winter looms.On Saturday, Zelenskyy condemned the White House's waiver of key provisions of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine.″... The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy said in a post on X. "And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people."Higher diesel prices – essential to transporting goods and agricultural production – tend to drive up costs across the wider economy and fuel inflation. With November's U.S. midterm elections approaching, Trump is under pressure to bring fuel costs down.But experts told CNBC that the diesel deal would deliver only a marginal financial benefit to Russia, and not move the needle much on global energy prices. Its wider political implications may be more significant, potentially reinforcing the Kremlin's belief that it can secure concessions from Washington without making compromises over Ukraine."Russia's main gain is political: Trump's decision eases sanctions pressure and undermines Western unity," Sergey Aleksashenko, senior research fellow and head of economics at the NEST Centre, told CNBC. Diesel dealTrump's agreement with Putin was for Russia to supply the global market with 4.8 million metric tons of diesel, the equivalent of about ten days of U.S. domestic demand, or about a single day of global demand. Experts say it will do little to affect prices."It does not even touch the sides – it is very, very small," Neil Atkinson, former head of the IEA's oil industry and markets division, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.watch nowAleksashenko estimated that the initial part of the phased agreement that covers 1.8 million metric tons of diesel could generate up to $1.25 billion in additional export revenue over three months, equivalent to around 1% of Russia's commodity export revenues during that period.However, the benefit to Russia's federal budget would be substantially smaller, at less than $30 million per month, or under 0.07% of monthly federal revenues.The deal was therefore unlikely to meaningfully strengthen Russia's war finances, Aleksashenko said. Instead, its main benefit to Moscow is political, because it eased sanctions pressure and undermined Western unity without requiring Putin to make concessions over Ukraine, he told CNBC.The research fellow also argued that the additional Russian diesel entering global markets is not sufficient to produce a noticeable reduction in consumer fuel prices in the short term."Funding the war is currently Putin's priority, and he is prepared to increase that funding even if it means cutting all other expenditures," Aleksashenko added, pointing to Russia's draft budget for 2027. The bigger problem for Ukraine"Rather than encouraging compromise, the [diesel] deal likely boosts Moscow's belief that continued pressure will eventually yield further Western concessions," Maria Snegovaya, senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC.Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy also warned that the diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives. "Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry."Earlier this week, reports emerged that SpaceX's Starlink military application Starshield has been restricted in Ukraine. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.The order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, according to a Reuters report citing three officials familiar with the matter. CNBC has contacted the White House for comment.The consequences were felt sharply in Ukraine. As Starlink's speed limits were lowered, Ukraine became incapable of shooting down some Russian drones. This week, Ukraine also did not receive advanced warning from partners of incoming ballistic missiles, resulting in civilian deaths, according to Ukrainian officials. According to Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, Starlink restrictions emboldened Russia to intensify attacks on Ukraine. "With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach told CNBC on Friday. Russian authorities didn't respond to multiple CNBC requests for comment.A political blowThe diesel deal was a political and moral blow to Ukraine and the Western coalition, according to Snegovaya. The U.S. sanctions exemption, which runs until April 2027, could facilitate Russian diesel exports beyond the initially announced shipment, potentially increasing Moscow's economic gains, she warned."If [the] White House uses its military and intelligence support as leverage to constrain Ukraine's strikes, the implications could become far more significant," Snegovaya said, adding that Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries have inflicted substantial economic costs on Moscow.Such a move could have far greater consequences for Ukraine's efforts to weaken Russia's war economy, she added.Read more of CNBC's Russia-Ukraine coverage:Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s energy ceasefire as drone attacks continueTrump declares ‘energy ceasefire’ between Russia and Ukraine; Zelenskyy is waiting for detailsUkraine’s surprise robot offensive exposes a vulnerability in Putin’s war machinePutin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy warns Russia preparing to deploy 10,000 North Korean troopsRussia ‘truly’ appreciates U.S. invite to G20 summit — but hasn’t decided if Putin will goZelenskyy says Ukraine ready for ‘energy ceasefire,’ calls for trilateral meeting with Putin, TrumpPutin floats ‘chance’ at peace with Ukraine as NATO chief warns Russia is becoming ‘increasingly reckless’Russia preparing ‘massive strikes’ on Ukraine’s energy sites after deadliest attack of the yearRussia's economy has defied the skeptics. Cracks are getting harder to hide'Winter is coming’: Ukraine fears its toughest test since Russia’s full-scale invasionThe diesel deal further undermines Washington's credibility as a mediator in the eyes of Ukraine and its European allies, as it appears to reward Moscow without securing concessions while increasing pressure on Kyiv, she said.The problem, Snegovaya said, is that achieving military autonomy for Europe and Ukraine is extremely difficult in the short term, and Europe has been slow to develop the necessary capabilities. "Almost five years into the war, Ukraine and its European partners remain heavily dependent on the U.S. in critical areas, like intelligence and missile defense. These dependencies are unlikely to be overcome during the remaining years of the Trump administration," she told CNBC.

schema.headline: Trump's Russia diesel deal may offer Putin more than money — and spell trouble for Ukraine
